result.topic_en: From Ramanujan's work on highly composite numbers: the form of numbers giving the maximum order of the generalized divisor function d_r(N), and the remark that these numbers approach the form of the least common multiple of the natural numbers as r tends to 0.
result.transcription:
Add Ms a 94 $^{18(38)}$ (38) (74)
and $d_r(N)$ of the form
(298) $(1+r)^{\pi(1+r)^x}(1+\frac{r}{2})^{\pi(1+\frac{r}{2})^x}(1+\frac{r}{3})^{\pi(1+\frac{r}{3})^x}\cdots\cdots$
From (297) and (298) we can easily find the maximum order of $d_r(N)$ as in §43.
It may be interesting to note that numbers of the form (297), which may also be written in the form
$e^{\vartheta\{x^{\frac{1}{r}\log(1+r)}\}+\vartheta\{x^{\frac{1}{r}\log(1+\frac{r}{2})}\}+\vartheta\{x^{\frac{1}{r}\log(1+\frac{r}{3})}\}+\cdots}$
approach the form
$e^{\vartheta(x)+\vartheta(\sqrt{x})+\vartheta(x^{1/3})+\cdots}$
as $r\to 0$. That is to say, they approach the form of the least common multiple of the natural numbers as $r\to 0$.

methods.what: Form of the numbers N that give the maximum order of the generalized divisor function d_r(N)
Determining the maximum order of d_r(N) from forms (297) and (298), by the method of §43

methods.what: Expression of the numbers of form (297) via Chebyshev's function theta
As r tends to 0, these numbers approach the least common multiple of 1..x, written as exp(theta(x)+theta(sqrt x)+theta(x^{1/3})+...)
